_what: A keyword table mapping the NAME of a matched database record to a coarse host group, and a concern weight for each group. It is a lookup table and nothing more: it reads the record's own organism string and the Pfam family of the protein, and says what that KNOWN record infects. It says nothing about the unidentified read that matched it.
_why_a_table_and_not_a_classifier: Taxonomy is not reachable from this container, and a learned classifier would put a model between a name and a label with no way for a reader to audit it. A table fires a named rule on every row, so the page can print 'grouped as bacteriophage because the name contains phage', and a reader can disagree with a specific line rather than with a black box.
_how_concern_is_meant: concern is a TRIAGE weight for ordering what a person looks at first, not a probability of harm, not a risk assessment, and not a clinical statement. It encodes one thing only: that a wastewater sequence resembling a vertebrate-infecting virus is worth a human's attention before one resembling a bacteriophage, because the plant is full of phage and that is the expected background.
_damping: Every weight is damped towards unknown by how far the match is. A relative at 95% identity over 100 amino acids transfers its host group; a relative at 40% over 30 does not. The damping is in concern_ranking.py and is shown on every card, because distance raises novelty interest and lowers host confidence at the same time and a score that hid that would be the project's own mistake in a new costume.

bacteriophage.label: bacteriophage
bacteriophage.reading: infects bacteria. The expected background of a wastewater RNA virome and the dominant signal in this library.

plant.label: plant
plant.reading: infects plants. Abundant in sewage from diet and runoff.

fungal_or_protist.label: fungal or protist
fungal_or_protist.reading: infects fungi, amoebae or other protists.

invertebrate.label: invertebrate
invertebrate.reading: infects insects or other invertebrates. Worth noting because arbovirus relatives sit here and because an insect virus in sewage is ordinary.

vertebrate_non_human.label: non-human vertebrate
vertebrate_non_human.reading: infects vertebrates other than humans. Livestock and wildlife viruses, which is where most spillover ancestry sits.

human_associated.label: human-associated
human_associated.reading: a family that includes viruses infecting humans. The group a person should look at first, and the one where the damping below matters most.

unknown_host.label: host not placed
unknown_host.reading: the table could not place this record's name. Weighted in the middle on purpose: an unplaceable name is not evidence of safety, and weighting it at zero would hide exactly the rows this project exists to find.

rules._why: a bare bacterial genus only implies a phage when the record came from the viral index. On a Swiss-Prot record it means the record is that bacterium: 'Bacillus subtilis ammonium transporter' was being grouped as a bacteriophage, which is how this condition came to be here.

_rule_order: Rules are tried in order and the first match wins, so the specific lines sit above the generic ones. A record naming both a bacterial genus and a phage is caught by the phage line first, which is the intended reading: 'Pseudomonas phage PaP2' infects Pseudomonas and is not Pseudomonas.
_coverage_is_reported: concern_ranking.py counts how many subjects no rule placed and writes it into ranking.json, because a table's blind spot is part of its result. A reader who sees a large unknown_host fraction should trust the ordering less, and the page prints it.
_why_bastrovirus_is_not_a_keyword: Bastroviruses are reported from human stool AND from bats, pigs and rats, so the genus name says nothing about a host and no single group is right for it. It is therefore not a keyword at all: a bastrovirus record is placed by the host word in its own name (Bat, Culex, Homo sapiens) or, failing that, by unknown_host, which is the honest answer. The name was briefly a vertebrate keyword as part of fixing the Astrovir substring bug; that overcorrected, because the fix the bug needed was the word boundary, not a reassignment.
_two_keyword_kinds: 'any' entries are prefixes anchored at the left only, so Picornavir catches Picornaviridae. 'word' entries are anchored at both ends, for host words that are substrings of ordinary English: bat must not fire on battery.

kind_rules._what: What KIND of thing the matched record is - a phage, some other virus, or something living. Separate from the host group, which says what that record infects. The two answer different questions and a row needs both.
kind_rules._the_hard_split: phage against bacterial is the hardest of the three and the page says so. Prophages sit inside bacterial genomes, so a protein can honestly be both, and at the identities in this residue - a few dozen amino acids at around half identity - neither the record nor the alignment settles it. These buckets describe the RECORD that was matched. They are not a call on the read.
kind_rules._phage_name_words_note: a NAME test, so a phage whose record does not say so lands in 'virus, nothing says phage'. That bucket is an absence of evidence and is labelled as one, never as 'not a phage'. Archaeal viruses land there too: they are viruses of prokaryotes but they are not bacteriophages and the page does not quietly call them one.

putative_phage.label: putative phage
putative_phage.reading: the matched record is a virus and its own name says phage

virus_no_phage_signal.label: virus, nothing says phage
virus_no_phage_signal.reading: the matched record is a virus from the viral index, and nothing in its name marks it as a phage. An absence of evidence, not a finding that it is not one

putative_bacterial.label: putative bacterial or archaeal
putative_bacterial.reading: the matched record is a protein of a named prokaryote, not of a virus. A prophage protein would look exactly like this

cellular_kind_not_placed.label: something living, kind not placed
cellular_kind_not_placed.reading: the record is a cellular protein and the table could not place its domain from the organism name

putative_eukaryotic.label: putative eukaryotic
putative_eukaryotic.reading: the matched record is a protein of a named plant, fungus, animal or protist. In a wastewater metatranscriptome this is diet, plant matter and the organisms living in the works, not a finding

kind_rules._host_group_on_a_cellular_record: a cellular record has no host: it IS the organism. The host group is therefore reported as not applicable on those rows rather than guessed, and they carry the unknown weight. The rules that place a name like Arabidopsis or Bacillus were written to read a VIRUS record's name, and letting them run on a Swiss-Prot entry turned a bacterium into a bacteriophage and a plant protein into a plant virus. Both were live until the kind axis was added.
